items.html:
Argentina uses two types of licence plates: a black one, which will be visible on street view with a black dot in the middle, and a white one with a blue bar at the top.

NOTE: The black dot can only be found on Argentinian licence plates, while the blue bar can be found in Brazil as well.

Argentina has a black Google car in Generation 3 coverage.

NOTE: Within South America, only Argentina, Peru and Uruguay have a black Google car.

Argentina also has Generation 4 “smallcam” coverage, which is mounted lower than regular Generation 4 and has a relatively big circular blur with a small protrusion at the front.

NOTE: Peru, Brazil and Argentina are the only South American countries with smallcam.

Round concrete poles sustaining three electricity lines in an alternating pattern are very common in Argentina.

Doubled up poles like in the second image is also a good clue for Argentina.

NOTE: Similar doubled concrete poles can occasionally be found throughout Bolivia.

Wooden poles are somewhat common in Argentina, they can be found either with a crossbar or without.

NOTE: Wooden A-frame poles in South America are only found in Argentina.

Argentina typically uses white-and-red chevrons.

NOTE: Argentina is the only American country with these chevrons.
Road lines in Argentina are mainly dashed white, double yellow or a mix in between.

Argentinian kilometre markers are typically white with a black strip displaying the road number at the top.

NOTE: The markers on national highways are indicated with RN, while RP indicates a provincial highway. National highways will be labelled white on the map, while provincial highways will be labelled green.

Yellow and red rectangular reflectors can often be seen on Argentinian guardrails.

NOTE: Within South America, they can also be found in Uruguay. However, Uruguayan guardrails can be differentiated from Argentinian guardrails by the shape of their support.

While Argentina features a plethora of different landscapes, most of the country is relatively flat, mostly treeless, and sparsely populated. In the absence of better clues, you should consider Argentina when you see landscapes like this with a very “wide open”, desolate feel.

These Argentinian cities have unique and recognisable taxis.

_You can click on the image to enlarge it._

Far western Argentina typically features a mountainous landscape.

NOTE: It is rare to find mountains in eastern Argentina.

Red soil is typically found in the Misiones province.

NOTE: Brazil and Argentina can look similar in this region. Make sure to look for other clues first.
In the Chaco and Formosa provinces, you will often see sandy soil with an abundance of vegetation; mainly low trees and bushes.
Grassland with a few separated tree plantations is generally found in this area.
Small lakes near the road are occasionally seen in the province of Buenos Aires.
Roads with reddish pavement lined with long Argentine needle-grass are common in San Luis.
Flat and barren landscapes like this are typically found in central southern Argentina.
If you see this kind of vegetation with flat grass and a low number of bushes, you are almost certainly in the state of Tierra del Fuego or southeastern Santa Cruz.

The majority of tree plantations in Argentina are located in the Entre Rios province.

NOTE: Uruguay and southern Brazil have them as well. Make sure to look at other clues before guessing.
Beech forests are commonly found in the state of Tierra del Fuego.

Coperinicia alba, also known as the Caranday Wax Palm, have short, fan-like leaves that tend to grow in low-density, single-species forests. Most common in Formosa, they can also be found in Chaco, Corrientes and northern Santa Fe.

Trithrinax Campestris, or the caranday palm, not to be confused with the Caranday Wax Palm, is a rustic palm native to the Sierras de Córdoba with a broader distribution in San Luis and northern mountainous Argentina. It can be identified by its compact fan-like leaves with a trunk hidden by a coat of dead-leaves.
The Butia yatay palm has arching, pinnate leaves and often grows at an incline with varying heights. It is most common in Corrientes and Parque Nacional El Palmar, Entre Rios.

The Totai Palm has small thin leaves with a visible spear shaped top, and a smooth trunk. It can be found as a decorational plant all across Argentina, however in the wild it is most common in Formosa, Chaco and Misiones.

Trichocereus atacamensis, or the cardón, is a cactus native to the high elevation mountain ranges of Catamarca, Tucumán, Salta and Jujuy. It can be identified by its candelabra-like appearance and fuzzy golden brown spines.

Stetsonia coryne, or the toothpick cactus, is a large tree-like cactus with many branches and spines resembling toothpicks. Its habitat includes a hotspot between Catamarca and Cordoba as well as the border area between Chaco, Salta and Formosa.
Wild sunflowers (Tithonia tubaeformis) are often found in Salta, Jujuy and Tucumán.

Prosopis caldenia, known as the caldén, is a decently large deciduous tree with small leaves and sinuous branches. It is mainly found in La Pampa.

NOTE: This tree can sometimes be confused with other trees such as the White Carob.
Pampas grass (Cortaderia selloana) is one of the most defining flora of the Pampas region. It is recognizable by its long bunched reeds and white fluffy flowerheads.
Sugarcane plantations are most common in Tucumán, with hotspots appearing in Salta and Jujuy.
Fields of sorghum can most commonly be seen in Santa Fe, Córdoba and Buenos Aires. It can be identified by its dark red flowerheads.
Corn fields can be found in most of northern Argentina, however they are most common in Córdoba and Santiago del Estero.
Fields of sunflowers are mainly found in southern Chaco, and less commonly in Buenos Aires and southern Córdoba.
Single rows of poplar trees, characterised by their thin and tall appearance, are very common around Neuquén. The area is also very flat.
Within Argentina, these Latvian style wooden hook poles are unique to La Rioja and Mendoza.
In Mendoza, poles with a single insulator attached to the side of the pole can be found.
White vertical pole stickers with several digits can be found in Tucumán.
You can find these unique markers on provincial roads in Cordoba.
T-Junctions in La Pampa sometimes have these yellow rectangular signs, with a chevron pattern on the bottom, and the Road Number(s) above, with an arrow on both sides.
Red bricks, similar to what is common in Bolivia, can be found in the northwest of the country, especially in western Jujuy.

In Mar Del Plata and surrounding cities (such as Miramar and Necochea), a unique style of architecture can be found. Its main features include quartzite stoned facades, orange tiled roofs, attached garages, and vault shaped porches.

Salt pans in Argentina are typically found in Jujuy.

NOTE: They can also be found in southwestern Bolivia and northeastern Chile.
These red mountains are unique to the RN68 valley in southern Salta.
These volcanic rocks in Generation 4 coverage can only be found on the RP43 south of Antofagasta de la Sierra in northwestern Catamarca.
The western part of the RN65 in western Tucumán can easily be recognized by this bendy unpaved road up in the mountains with its western part up in the clouds.
Red soil with a barren landscape and mountain ranges, can often be seen on the RN76 in Parque Nacional Talampaya in western La Rioja.

These mountains are typically found west of Córdoba.

NOTE: They are not as high as the mountains in the west.

This horse trekker can be found in southwestern San Juan.

NOTE: A similar trekker can be found on the other side in Chile.

If you see vineyards with mountains in the west and flatness in the east, you are most likely in the outskirts of Mendoza.

NOTE: There are multiple wine regions in Argentina, but the Mendoza wine region is the most recognisable one of them all.
Semi-coastal grass hills are seen in southern Buenos Aires, especially northeast of Bahía Blanca.

The monkey puzzle tree can be found in western Neuquen. The most specimens are seen on state road 23.

NOTE: They are seen on the other side in Chile as well.
The “sawdust” car is found in centre-south Argentina and has a unique sandy dust on its visible black back.

Villa Dique Florentino Ameghino in northeastern Chubut is surrounded by these rock formations.

NOTE: Sometimes you will be able to see this dam in the west.
Comodoro Rivadavia is built on the slopes of Chenque hill, making the city recognisable.
Melting snow coverage is seen on the eastern RN293 close to the Chilean border in southwestern Santa Cruz.

These snowy mountains to the north can only be found in Ushuaia.

NOTE: Ushuaia is the southernmost city of Argentina and the province capital of Tierra del Fuego.

steps.html:
GeoGuessr’s own official Argentina map is not very good, for a variety of reasons. Plonk It recommends the following maps instead:

  • An Arbitrary Argentina (map link) - Over 100k well balanced computer generated locations around Argentina.
  • AI Gen - Argentina (map link) - 50k+ generated locations.

In addition, here are some resources to help you practise Argentina:

  • Plonk It Argentina (map link) - This map contains locations for practising each meta in the Plonk It Argentina guide from step 2 to 3.

  • Rio Negro on the roads Chasico-Laguna Blanca and Chasico-Ingeniero Jacobacci
  • Chubut in the area between Paso del Sapo and Gobernador Costa

lm.name: Vegetation - Poplar Plantation - Mediterranean
lm.note:
Poplar Trees are thin and tall decidiuous trees. They can be found all over Argentina.

If you see them planted in single rows accompanied by hilly to mountainous, mediterranean landscape, as well as mediterranean agriculture (e.g. vineyards and olives) and vegetation (e.g. palm trees, platanus trees), you are likely in a town or city in the provinces of Mendoza and San Juan.

lm.name: Vegetation - Red Baron
lm.note:
Red Baron is a grass species that has a very distinctive red hue. It's found in

  • Western and Southern Santa Cruz
  • Northwestern Chubut
  • Southern Neuquen

lm.name: Vegetation - Red Baron - Dense
lm.note:
Red Baron is a grass species that has a very distinctive red hue.

In very dense assemblages, it can appear here:

  • Max South Santa Cruz, latitudes south of Rio Gallegos
  • The national 40 north of Las Horquetas (Santa Cruz)
  • The national 40 between Esquel and Estanzia Nueva Lubecka

lm.name: Vegetation - Single Row Poplar - Flat
lm.note:
Poplar Trees are thin and tall decidiuous trees. They can be found all over Argentina.

If you see them planted in a single row and accompanied by a very flat landscape, you are in one of these places:

  • National 22 between Neuquen and Choele Choel (Rio Negro)
  • Trelew (Chubut)
  • Sarmiento (Chubut)

lm.name: Catamarca red mountains
lm.note: On the 60, east of Fiambalá, bright red mountains line the road, sometimes quite dramatically. A few of the red hills are embedded in between gray hills in a way that almost looks like a badly colored black and white photograph. Good luck telling it apart from similar roads in Salta and La Rioja! The best method may be the clouds: This road has no clouds, while the one in La Rioja has some low hazy ones to the South (except when it doesn't) and the one in Salta has higher, better defined clouds. It's tough.

lm.name: La Rioja red mountains
lm.note: In La Rioja, just north of Talampaya National Park, there is a part of the RN40 with almost blindingly bright red mountains. Good luck telling it apart from similar roads in Catamarca and Salta! The best method may be the clouds: This road has low clouds toward the South (except when it doesn't), while the one in Catamarca is always cloudless and the one in Salta has higher, better defined clouds. It's tough.

lm.name: Neuqén sunrise
lm.note: In the North of Neuquén, the Google driver started their day early and the camera did not like it. As the day progresses, the car goes further north and the glitchy colors fade, until only a bit of color noise remains, and finally, around the province border, it starts to look like normal footage.

lm.name: Salta red mountains
lm.note: On the 68 in Salta, between Alemania and Cafayate, there's a stretch of red mountains. Compared to the red mountains in La Rioja and Catamarca, the surrounding range is more massive and the red not quite as cartoonish. You may also be able to tell the difference by the clouds: The ones here are high above and relatively defined; the ones in La Rioja, when they appear, are low in the southern sky and kind of hazy, and the coverage in Catamarca is cloudless.

lm.name: Tucuman mist road
lm.note: On the 65 in Tucuman, leading west to the Catamarca border near Parque Nacional Aconquija, the Google car drove through what appears to be mist thick enough to clog your windpipe.

lm.name: Roadlines
lm.note: • Road lines in Argentina are mainly dashed white, double yellow or a mix in between.

lm.name: Argentina
lm.note: Phone Codes in Argentina are 10 digits, with the 3 ou 4 firsts digit wich are regionals (2 for Buenos Aires).

lm.name: Argentina Wild Sunflowers
lm.note: Wild sunflowers (Verbesina encelioides) are often found in Salta, Jujuy and Tucumán.

lm.name: Argentine Tree Plantations
lm.note: Along the border with Uruguay in Entre Rios and Corrientes is where you'll most commonly find tree plantations in Argentina. There may be others rarely in other parts of these provinces/Argentina.

lm.name: Bariloche
lm.note: Bariloche is a famous resort town in Nuequen. It can be recognized by the ski town vibes, the lake, and the mountains. While there are some other similar towns in Southern Argentina, Bariloche stands out and can be recognized with practice!

lm.name: Boat Coverage Entre Rios
lm.note: Just north of Buenos Aires City near Villa Paranacito there is boat coverage that is recognizable with the foliage and sometimes visible architecture.

lm.name: Buenos Aires Black and Yellow Taxi
lm.note: Black taxis with yellow rooftops can be seen commonly in the capital of Buenos Aires. While they should be unique to Buenos Aires Similar but distint taxis can be found in other cities.

lm.name: Buenos Aires Small Ponds
lm.note: Small ponds near the road are occasionally seen in the province of Buenos Aires.

lm.name: Cardon Cacti
lm.note: Trichocereus atacamensis, or the cardón, is a cactus native to the high elevation mountain ranges of Catamarca, Tucumán, Salta and Jujuy. It can be identified by its candelabra-like appearance and fuzzy golden brown spines.

lm.name: Chaco/Formosa - Sandy Soil and Vegetation
lm.note: In the Chaco and Formosa provinces, you will often see sandy soil with an abundance of vegetation; mainly low trees and bushes.

lm.name: Comodoro Rivadavia
lm.note: Comodoro Rivadavia is built on the slopes of Chenque hill, making the city recognisable.

lm.name: Cordoba Taxis
lm.note: Taxis in Cordoba are often all yellow or all green. May be seen uncommonly in other towns but if you're in a very large city with similar taxis it's likely Cordoba.

lm.name: Eastern Santa Cruz Snow Coverage
lm.note: Snow coverage is found on the eastern RP25 in eastern Santa Cruz.

lm.name: Green Hills of Buenos Aires
lm.note: Semi-coastal grass hills are seen in southern Buenos Aires, especially northeast of Bahía Blanca.

lm.name: Jujuy Province
lm.note: The northern province of Jujuy has unique architecture similar to that of the brick buildings in Bolivia and Peru.

lm.name: La Pampa T-Intersection Sign
lm.note: T-Junctions in La Pampa sometimes have these usually yellow (rarely other colors) rectangular signs, with a chevron pattern on the bottom, usually the Road Number(s) above, with an arrow on both sides.

lm.name: Latvian Style Hook Poles
lm.note: Within Argentina, these Latvian style wooden hook poles are unique to La Rioja and Mendoza. (A bit more common in La Rioja, which also has a drier, more desert-like feel)

lm.name: Misiones Red Soil
lm.note: The soil in misiones is a distinct red color (similar to the Brazil across the border). This combined with the vegetation in the area can be a good clue for this region.

lm.name: Monkey Puzzle Tree
lm.note:
The monkey puzzle tree can be found in western Neuquen. The most specimens are seen on state road 23.

NOTE: They are seen on the other side in Chile as well.

lm.name: Pampas Grass
lm.note: Pampas grass (Cortaderia selloana) is one of the most defining flora of the Pampas region. It is recognizable by its long bunched reeds and white fluffy flowerheads.

lm.name: Pink Trumpet Tree
lm.note: The Pink Trumpet Tree (Handroanthus impetiginosus) can be found in cities in northern Salta such as Orán, Tartagal, General Mosconi and Salvador Mazza.

lm.name: RN40 Low-Quality Sunset
lm.note: Sunset coverage with degraded image quality is found on the RN40 just south of the Mendoza border with Neuquén.

lm.name: RN68 Red Mountains
lm.note: These red mountains are unique to the RN68 valley in southern Salta.

lm.name: San Luis
lm.note: Roads with reddish pavement lined with long Argentine needle-grass are common in San Luis.

lm.name: South-Central Saw Dust Car
lm.note: The “sawdust” car is found in centre-south Argentina (mostly west Rio Negro) and has a unique sandy dust on its visible black back.

lm.name: Southern Argentina
lm.note: If you see this kind of vegetation with flat grass and a low number of bushes, you are almost certainly in the state of Tierra del Fuego or southeastern Santa Cruz.

lm.name: Sugarcane
lm.note: Sugarcane plantations are most common in Tucumán, with hotspots appearing in Salta and Jujuy.

lm.name: The caldén
lm.note: Prosopis caldenia, known as the caldén, is a decently large deciduous tree with small leaves and sinuous branches. It is mainly found in La Pampa.

lm.name: Toothpick Cactus
lm.note: Stetsonia coryne, or the toothpick cactus, is a large tree-like cactus with many branches and spines resembling toothpicks. Its habitat includes a hotspot between Catamarca and Cordoba as well as the border area between Chaco, Salta and Formosa.

lm.name: Tucuman Pole Stickers
lm.note: White vertical pole stickers with several digits can be found in Tucumán.

lm.name: Ushuaia
lm.note: The southernmost city of Argentina, Ushuaia, is easily recognizable by the snowy mountains to the north, the archictecture, and the vegetation.

lm.name: Ushuaia Region - Tierra Del Fuego
lm.note: Well forested mountainous areas around Ushuaia in Southern Tierra Del Fuego are easily recognized.

lm.name: Valdes Peninsula Wide Dirt Roads
lm.note: Unusually wide dirt roads and flat geography make the Valdes peninsula of Eastern Chubut recognizable.

lm.name: Villa Dique Florentino
lm.note: Villa Dique Florentino Ameghino in northeastern Chubut is surrounded by these rock formations.

lm.name: Lushly Forested and Mountainous Landscape -  West Arg
lm.note:
This landscape is mainly characterized by:

  • forested, high and rocky mountains
  • lush vegetation;
  • predominance of pine trees, spruce trees and larches; glacial lakes;

lm.name: Azorella Prolifera - Cushion-looking plant
lm.note: Azorella Prolifera is a light green cushion-looking plant with tiny yellow flowers. This plant may be found throughout the Patagonia region. However, as it was said, the appearance (talking mainly about hue) of shrubs and other plants depends on the month/season. The season that provides such a look is late spring or early summer.

lm.name: Cabo Blanco - Lighthouse
lm.note: Cabo Blanco can be recognized by this rock with a lighthouse.

lm.name: Caviahue Copahue - Snow coverage + Mountains
lm.note: Snowy mountains with cloudy mountain tops and dark dirt road

lm.name: Central and Eastern Dirt Roads  - April
lm.note:
The April autumn may be tricky and sometimes hard to recognize. April on the east coast looks like a mix of March and June, like… it kinda looks like winter coverage but it’s not really it.

April has additional two different appearances:

  • Comodoro Rivadavia hills in April coverage (may look like March);
  • mostly cloudy + visible mountain range in the distance to the north;

lm.name: Central and Eastern Dirt Roads  - December
lm.note: The December summer landscape in Chubut looks very distinctive mainly because of the characteristic light soil and green shrubland. That type of landscape is also mentioned in another meta called “Very Green Shrubland”.

lm.name: Central and Eastern Dirt Roads  - Jan,Feb,Mar
lm.note:
The January, February and March summer generally looks very sunny, dry with greenish shrubs.

These months look identical. However, March has additional three different appearances:

  • very dry-looking March;
  • Península Valdés landscape;
  • cloudy March;

lm.name: Central and Eastern Dirt Roads  - June
lm.note: The June winter almost everywhere looks the same or very similar. However, there is a small stretch of RP1 between Rawson and Puerto Madryn on which you can find a June sunrise coverage.

lm.name: Central and Eastern Dirt Roads  - October
lm.note:
The October spring may be quite hard to recognize at the first time but after some practicing, it will be recognizable easily. The green color of shrubland in October has such distinctive vibes. The shrubland is like a mix of shrubs that have vivid green color and weak green color with greenish grass.

October has additional two different appearances:

  • cloudy with a characteristic rain cloud;
  • october coverage looking like a summer;

lm.name: Central and Eastern Dirt Roads  - September
lm.note: The September spring is quite easy to recognize because of the cloudy coverage, greenish shrubland and vegetation which looks kinda autumnal.

lm.name: Cerro Policía - Distinct Plateau
lm.note:
Cerro Policía is a village located in north-western(ish) Rio Negro. To easily tell that you are in the nearby area, look for this very distinctive plateau:

This can be recognized from a distance from the whitish spots on the plateau

lm.name: Dirty Car - Rio Negro
lm.note: The “dirty back of the car” is the most popular car meta in Argentina. This car meta is exclusive for the northwestern(ish) part of Rio Negro province

lm.name: Dr. Atilio Oscar Viglione - Rainbow
lm.note: This village has a very unique appearance because of both the rainbow to the south and a big-looking sun to the north

lm.name: Eastern Neuqeun - Neuquen Soil?
lm.note:
Generally, in the eastern Neuquén (east of the RN40) it is very common to see reddish/maroon soil.

  • Only exception is the RP5 in Rio Negro.
  • Mind that in the northern provinces such a landscape may also occur there but predominantly you can additionally see small trees mixed with such a landscape.
  • Mind that, the similar color of soil may also be found in the northern provinces e.g. La Rioja, Salta. But in Neuquén the soil usually is accompanied by a very specific landscape, shrub-steppe landscape mixed with branchy shrubs.

In conclusion: Reddish/maroon soil + shrub-steppe landscape mixed with branchy shrubs = eastern Neuquén.

lm.name: Eastern Rio Negro - Lush green landscape and light soil
lm.note:
As we can see, the eastern Rio Negro is mainly accompanied by a lush green vegetation, shrublands mixed with a grass and a light soil. Additionally, let’s pay attention to the trees. In Rio Negro province the Neuquen trees (thin and tall ones) are only seen along the Rio Negro river which connects Viedma and Neuquen cities.

The area where you can see the eastern Rio Negro landscape is marked in green whereas the Rio Negro river - as a red line.

It is worth adding that the northern Rio Negro (north of the river) does have a similar appearance to the eastern Rio Negro landscape but the northern part is less lush than the generic eastern part.

lm.name: El Maitén - Mountain Range
lm.note: El Maitén is a town located in north-western Chubut province. To easily tell that you are in this town area or nearby, look for this very distinctive mountain range to the east:

lm.name: Gobernador Gregores - North hills
lm.note: Gobernador Gregores is a town located in the central Santa Cruz province. The area near this town is very green with lots of trees and wetlands. To easily tell that you are in this town area, look for these distinctive green hills to the north:

lm.name: Grass - TDF, South Santa Cruz
lm.note: The grass-steppe landscape is characterized by a grassy landscape consisting of tufts of grass and tiny shrubs. Grass-steppe landscape also is characterized by a complete lack of bushes and trees.

lm.name: High Branchy Shrubs - Central-Northern Rio Negro
lm.note: With fields of these high branchy shrubs it is more likely that you are in the part of Rio Negro shown below(refer to the 2nd image):

lm.name: Monkey Puzzle - Western Neuquén
lm.note: Araucaria Araucana (also known as Monkey Puzzle Tree) is a species of evergreen coniferous tree found only in the central-western Neuquén province near the Chilean border.

lm.name: Mountainous Neuquén - Dry mountains, exposed rock
lm.note: This type of landscape is typical of summer coverage. The Mountainous Neuquén Landscape is characterized by dry mountains with exposed rocks. There is also a large number of rivers, therefore, it’s very likely to see lots of poplar trees and bushes in the valleys. Additionally, in some places, the groves of small coniferous trees occur.

lm.name: No Center - RP5, RP50, RP11
lm.note: Outer solid white lines no center line (only applies in gen 3)

lm.name: Northeast Santa Cruz - Shrub-Steppe Landscape
lm.note:
Northeastern Santa Cruz shrub-steppe landscape is characterized by:

  • cloudy coverage;
  • dark brownish soil dirt roads;
  • tufts of grass and dark green shrubs;

lm.name: Northern Santa cruz - Tiny shrubs + yellowish grass
lm.note: Northern Santa Cruz landscape is dry and is mainly accompanied by tiny shrubs + tufts of yellowish grass. Also, you can see hills and plateaus in the distance both to the south and to the north mostly always (this coverage can be gen 4).

lm.name: Northwest Chubut - May
lm.note:
Northwestern Chubut landscape in May (late autumn coverage) looks very unique. This landscape is characterized by:

  • rocky soil;
  • very large number of small coniferous and deciduous trees;
  • sunny autumnal and mountainous landscape (trees and bushes with red and orange leaves + snow-capped mountains);

lm.name: Península Valdés - Wide road
lm.note:
The distinctive features of Península Valdés Landscape are:

  • wide dirt roads (for the Peninsula itself);
  • tight sandy soil;
  • tiny yellowish grass;
  • green shrubs;

lm.name: Piedra Parada - Colossal Rock
lm.note: Piedra Parada is known for its very famous colossal rock which resulted from a volcanic eruption many millions years ago. The rock is a part of the national park which is characterized by a very rocky landscape.

lm.name: Poplars - Neuquen/Trelew
lm.note: Poplars are thin and tall deciduous trees that are mainly associated with the Neuquén province - hence the common name. These trees may be found in many different places in Argentina so they are not province exclusive. However, if you see lots of poplars that are single-row planted and are accompanied by a very flat landscape* then it’s very likely that you are either in the town of Trelew (eastern Chubut province), town of Sarmiento (southern Chubut province) or in cities/towns along the Río Negro river that connects Neuquen and Viedma cities.

lm.name: Puerto San Julian - Hills
lm.note:
Puerto San Julian is a town located in the central-eastern Santa Cruz province. To easily tell that you are nearby, look for these two distinctive hills (refer to the 1st image)

These hills may be visible when you are in the area marked in green, black dots are where approximately where the hillls are (refer to the 2nd image).

lm.name: Red Baron - Red hue
lm.note: Imperata Cylindrica “Red Baron” is a grass species that has a very distinctive red hue. This grass may be found throughout the Patagonia region but only in the west (western Rio Negro, western Chubut etc.). Sometimes Imperata Cylindrica may occur in very dense assemblages as shown on the first and on the second image. However, there are not many places with dense assemblages of this grass - these may be found only in the western Chubut plus southern and central Santa Cruz provinces.

lm.name: Rio Negro shrubland - Río Negro, south La Pampa
lm.note: This type of landscape is typical of summer coverage. The Río Negro Shrubland is characterized by green shrubs and bushes, tiny/long yellowish and greenish grass plus light soil. However, the most important aspect of this landscape is the fact that there is an almost complete lack of trees. Trees may only be found near the Río Negro river.

lm.name: RP - 6 - No road lines
lm.note: This section of the RP-6 has an asphalt road with no road lines.

lm.name: RP - 61 - Protruding Rock
lm.note: This road has a distinctive-looking protruding rock from a mountain.

lm.name: RP - 63
lm.note:
Generally, RP63 shares a very specific landscape so the road should be very easy to recognize. The landscape is characterized by:

  • lush and green vegetation (shrub-steppes, bushes and trees);
  • rolling high and very rocky mountains;
  • diverse rock formations on the mountainsides;

lm.name: RP - 69
lm.note:
RP-69

  • The more west you go on this road, the more you can see mountains almost fully covered in snow (refer to the top image)
  • The rest of this road can be recognized by a hilly landscape, everything looking brown, and the sunny coverage with a dirt road (not unique, but might rule out other roads, refer to the bottom image)

lm.name: RP - 7
lm.note: Random blurs + sunrise

lm.name: RP - 7 Mountain in Neuquen

lm.name: RP - 7 Plateau in Neuquen
lm.note:
This road has a distinctive plateau to the north

Other characteristics: brownish-maroon soil (or neuquen soil), dirt road

lm.name: RP - 71 - Mountain Range

lm.name: RP - 71 - Rainy coverage
lm.note: Characteristics: asphalt road, rainy coverage, some bright smudges in front

lm.name: RP - 71 - Sewer
lm.note: Road sewer along the forested dirt road

lm.name: RP - 74 - Powerlines
lm.note:
This road can be recognized the powerlines that are along the entire road.

Other characteristics: dirt road, looks like Santa Cruz May coverage (there are other roads in Patagonia with powerlines going along it, so use the other characteristics to tell them apart)

lm.name: RP - 75 & 1
lm.note: This is an asphalt road with rainy/rainy clouds coverage

RP8 has 3 different sky appearances whereas RP5 has a single one. Every color on a map indicates from where were the images below taken:

lm.name: RP - 9 - Badlands
lm.note:
This road has can be separated to 2 stretches with distinct badlands:

  • The part shaded in green can be recognized by distinct reddish badlands(Example in the 1st image)
  • The part not shaded in green can be recognized by these distinct badlands to the west(refer to the 2nd image)

lm.name: RP - 97
lm.note: This road can be recognized by a dirt road with gray gravel + dark brownish soil

lm.name: RP - 99
lm.note: Dirt road with distinctive hills to the west

lm.name: RP - Monkey puzzles (1)
lm.note: Characteristics: Very forested and mountainous landscape with lots of monkey puzzle trees (monkey puzzles can be found in other roads, but the other characteristics can distinguish them enough).

lm.name: RP - Monkey puzzles (2)
lm.note: Characteristics: dirt road and a mountainous landscape with lots of monkey puzzle trees(monkey puzzles can be found in other roads, but the other characteristics can distinguish them enough).

lm.name: RP - Protruding rock
lm.note:
A protruding rock on a plateau can be seen in the green shaded area in the RP-10.

Other characteristics: dirt road, brownish-maroon soil, sky (the further north, the more cloudy it gets)

lm.name: San Jorge - Hills
lm.note: These smooth hills covered by a large number of small shrubs (branchy shrubs) and light sandy soil are distinctive to the San Jorge Gulf area.

lm.name: Sarmiento - Smudge
lm.note: One smudge on the ground meta, this can be seen throughout the entire town

lm.name: Shrub Steppes - Central-Western Rio Negro
lm.note: With this shrub-steppe landscape you should be in central-western part of Rio Negro. Approximate area(refer to the 2nd image):

lm.name: Sierra Colorada - Brownish Hills
lm.note: To easily tell that you are in the nearby area of this village, look for these very distinctive dark-brownish/red soil smooth hills (example):

lm.name: Small Mountain - Northeast, Distinctive
lm.note: There is a small mountain in the northeastern Neuquén province whose shape is very distinctive and visible from roads around it:

lm.name: South TDF - Autumn
lm.note: The southern Tierra del Fuego is unique and characterized by: cloudy autumn coverage; grass-steppe landscape; forests consisting of small deciduous and coniferous trees; some dead trees lying on ground (first image);

lm.name: TDF Pipe - RN3
lm.note: Pipe along the road

lm.name: Unnamed Road Chubut - West of Trevelin
lm.note: Can be recognized by it's wet looking road, May coverage

lm.name: Unnamed Road Neuquen - Brown-maroon soil
lm.note: This is a dirt road that has brown-maroon soil, this soil can be seen on other roads, however the tint can be distinctive + the dirt road, a majority of this road also has dirt on the sides that goes a bit higher than the road (I don't know what it's called and I'm sorry if this description is confusing). Water can be seen on the stretches of road near the lake.

lm.name: Ushuaia - Snowy Mountains
lm.note: These snowy mountains to the north can only be found in Ushuaia.

lm.name: Very green shrubland - December
lm.note: This landscape, which is typical of December coverage, is characterized by a shrubland consisting of very green shrubs, tiny yellowish grass and very light soil.

lm.name: Villa Dique Florentino Ameghino - Unique Rocky Landscape
lm.note: This village has a unique rocky landscape so it’s very easy to recognize both the village and the nearby area

lm.name: White Car - Neuquén Spill
lm.note: The white car, as a spillover, in Neuquén may be found on RN231 in the southern part of the province:art of the province:

lm.name: Buenos Aires - Small Lakes
lm.note: Small lakes near the road are occasionally seen in the province of Buenos Aires.

lm.name: Butia Yatay Palm - Corrientes and Parque Nacional El Palmar
lm.note: The Butia yatay palm has arching, pinnate leaves and often grows at an incline with varying heights. It is most common in Corrientes and Parque Nacional El Palmar, Entre Rios.

lm.name: Caranday Palm - Sierras de Córdoba
lm.note: Trithrinax Campestris, or the caranday palm, not to be confused with the Caranday Wax Palm, is a rustic palm native to the Sierras de Córdoba with a broader distribution in San Luis and northern mountainous Argentina. It can be identified by its compact fan-like leaves with a trunk hidden by a coat of dead-leaves.

lm.name: Caranday Wax Palm - Chaco, Corrientes and northern Santa Fe.
lm.note: Coperinicia alba, also known as the Caranday Wax Palm, have short, fan-like leaves that tend to grow in low-density, single-species forests. Most common in Formosa, they can also be found in Chaco, Corrientes and northern Santa Fe.

lm.name: Cardon - Catamarca, Tucumán, Salta and Jujuy.
lm.note: Trichocereus atacamensis, or the cardón, is a cactus native to the high elevation mountain ranges of Catamarca, Tucumán, Salta and Jujuy. It can be identified by its candelabra-like appearance and fuzzy golden brown spines.

lm.name: Central Argentina - Flat, barren landscape
lm.note: Flat and barren landscapes like this are typically found in central southern Argentina.

lm.name: Chaco and Formosa - Sandy Soil
lm.note: In the Chaco and Formosa provinces, you will often see sandy soil with an abundance of vegetation; mainly low trees and bushes.

lm.name: Corn - Córdoba, Buenos Aires and Santiago del Estero.
lm.note: Corn fields can be found in most of northern Argentina, however they are most common in Córdoba, Buenos Aires and Santiago del Estero.

lm.name: Entre Rios - Tree Plantations
lm.note:
The majority of tree plantations in Argentina are located in the Entre Rios province.

NOTE: Uruguay and southern Brazil have them as well. Make sure to look at other clues before guessing.

lm.name: La Pampa - Caldén and grid
lm.note:
Prosopis caldenia, known as the caldén, is a decently large deciduous tree with small leaves and sinuous branches. It is mainly found in La Pampa.

Extra meta: A lot of roads in La Pampa are in a grid (meaning exactly North, South, East, West) which can be a good meta for this province (It's rare for roads outside La Pampa to be in a grid)

lm.name: Macaw Palm - Formosa, Chaco and Misiones.
lm.note: The Macaw Palm has small thin leaves with a visible spear shaped top. It can be found as a decorational plant all across Argentina, however in the wild it is most common in Formosa, Chaco and Misiones.

lm.name: Misiones - Red Soil
lm.note: Red soil is typically found in the Misiones province.

lm.name: Pampas Grass - Pampas Region
lm.note: Pampas grass (Cortaderia selloana) is one of the most defining flora of the Pampas region. It is recognizable by its long bunched reeds and white fluffy flowerheads.

lm.name: Salta, Jujuy, Tucuman - Wild Sunflowers
lm.note: Wild sunflowers (Tithonia tubaeformis) are often found in Salta, Jujuy and Tucumán.

lm.name: San Luis - Needle Grass
lm.note:
Roads with reddish pavement lined with long Argentine needle-grass are common in San Luis.

Creator note:not all locations will have the reddish pavement but will still have the Argentine needle-grass which from experience is pretty reliable for getting San Luis

lm.name: Sugarcane - Tucumán
lm.note: Sugarcane plantations are most common in Tucumán, with hotspots appearing in Salta and Jujuy.

lm.name: TDF - Beech Forests
lm.note: Beech forests are commonly found in the state of Tierra del Fuego.

lm.name: TDF and Southern Santa Cruz - Flat grass
lm.note: If you see this kind of vegetation with flat grass and a low number of bushes, you are almost certainly in the state of Tierra del Fuego or southeastern Santa Cruz.

lm.name: Toothpick Cactus - Catamara, Cordoba and the border of Chaco, Salta, and Formosa
lm.note: Stetsonia coryne, or the toothpick cactus, is a large tree-like cactus with many branches and spines resembling toothpicks. Its habitat includes a hotspot between Catamarca and Cordoba as well as the border area between Chaco, Salta and Formosa.

lm.name: Western Argentina - Mountains
lm.note: Far western Argentina typically features a mountainous landscape.

lm.name: Roadlines
lm.note: • Road lines in Argentina are mainly dashed white, double yellow or a mix in between.

lm.name: Antofagasta de la Sierra
lm.note:
Where : northern Catamarca, south of Antofagasta de la Sierra, RP43

Description : South starts out as dry and has rocky mountains that are sandy. As the road continues it becomes high altitude and accumulates dark volcanic rock/gravel. The north is particularly distinct with lower clouds.

lm.name: Catamarca
lm.note: Description : Catamarca has a big ridge east and a big ridge west, with an open valley to the south and hills to the north sometimes visible.

lm.name: Cerro El Morro
lm.note:
Where : northeastern San Luis, north of Villa Mercedes, around Cerro El Morro

Description : Landscape is quite flat except for a seemingly random mountain in the middle of nowhere which is very distinct.

lm.name: Cerro Nevado
lm.note:
Where : central Mendoza, south of San Rafael, roads around Cerro Nevado

Description : Very distinct snow-capped ridge can be seen from very far.

lm.name: Comodoro Rivadavia
lm.note: Description : Comodoro Rivadavia is a very hilly coastal town, surrounded by distinct limestone mountains, the main city is mostly Gen4 and the outskirts mostly Gen3.

lm.name: Comodoro Rivadavia hills
lm.note:
Where : southeastern Chubut, west of Comodoro Rivadavia

Description : East-west valleys with small hills, green southern vegetation and low sun hidden behind the ridges. Occasionally it can have snow too.

lm.name: El Cain
lm.note:
Where : central Rio Negro, around El Cain, RP8 & RP5

Description : overcast gen3 road, winter coverage.

lm.name: Iruya
lm.note:
Where : northern Salta, south of Iruya, RP133

Description : Very distinct dry mountains with slight pink/tan rock and almost looks as if somebody cut them with a knife or took a bite out.

lm.name: La Rioja
lm.note: Description : La Rioja has a very close ridge going north to south to the west, and flatness to the east and the south.

lm.name: Lago Salinas Grande
lm.note:
Where : southern Catamarca, around the Lago Salinas Grandes, RN60/157

Description : Pinkish brown soil that is dried out and flat with green bushes on either side. Abundance of cacti. Certain areas are quite barren particularly where the map shows water. Road angle is useful to confirm.

lm.name: Las Leñas
lm.note:
Where : southwestern Mendoza, east of Las Leñas, RP222

Description : Massive front blur and distinct snow poles. The road runs along a dried up river bed with light green vegetation.

lm.name: Mendoza
lm.note:
Description : Mendoza has very big mountains to the west, with not real elevation to the east. Vineyards and winter coverage are very common.

It is very easy to confuse with San Juan, however a ridge can be seen in the east in San Juan (which is not obvious on every loc, so sending the wrong one is pretty common).

lm.name: Nazareno
lm.note:
Where : northern Salta, near Nazareno, RP69

Description : Very narrow, dangerous-looking road and high altitude. Looks very similar to some roads seen in Peru.

lm.name: Parque Nacional Los Cardones
lm.note:
Where : central Salta, around Parque Nacional Los Cardones

Description : Dry open valleys with Cardon cacti spam.

lm.name: Parque Nacional Talampaya
lm.note:
Where : central La Rioja, around and in Parque Nacional Talampaya, RN76

Description : Very wide open valley with distant reddish mountains and some of the most distinct pink sandy soil in the country.

lm.name: Posadas
lm.note: Description : Posadas is the biggest town in Misiones, with a very consistent grid going ESE. The town is a bit hilly.

lm.name: Rio Gallegos
lm.note:
Description : Rio Gallegos has a pretty consistent grid and Gen4 snowy coverage in the town.

In Gen3 it is very easy to mistake it for Rio Grande, in Tierra del Fuego.

lm.name: RN101 (paved)
lm.note:
Where : northern Misiones, east of Puerto Iguazú, RN101

Description : Classic misiones brownish road but with danish road lines (outside and inside) between the crossroad with the RN12 and the airport, only place with those road lines in Misiones.

lm.name: RN101 (unpaved)
lm.note:
Where : northern Misiones, east of Puerto Iguazú, RN101

Description : Unpaved E-W road with very overgrown Brazilian looking vegetation. Road is wetter in the west.

lm.name: RN12
lm.note:
Where : northern Corrientes, west of Posadas, RN12

Description : Big tree plantations (sometimes very far), Misiones-looking reddish road (but without a classic Misiones landscape).

lm.name: RN14
lm.note:
Where : eastern Entre Rios, southern Corrientes, RN14

Description : Divided highway until Paso de los Libres (under Uruguaiana label), only highway with this angle in those two provinces, tree plantations, yellow inner line.

lm.name: RN141
lm.note:
Where : eastern San Juan, east of San Juan, RN141

Description : Distinct big flat ridge north that appears to taper at one end. Sometimes a small ridge can be seen far south.

lm.name: RN149
lm.note:
Where : southern San Juan, south of Barreal, RN149

Description : Very open valley, ridges in all directions, paved in the San Juan part, unpaved in Mendoza (the ridges are further away than the RP412 in San Juan). Clouds sit almost only on top of the mountains giving a distinct look.

lm.name: RN150
lm.note:
Where : northern San Juan, west of San José de Jachal, RN150

Description : East to west valley, exposed dark rock is common and sun behind the ridges. Looks vaguely like mountains seen in Oman/UAE, but darker.

lm.name: RN150
lm.note:
Where : western San Juan, west of Las Flores, RN150

Description : East to west valley, exposed dark rocky mountains and melting snow the further west you go.

lm.name: RN151
lm.note:
Where : western La Pampa, south of Santa Isabel, RN151

Description : Very flat, paved road with small bushes, you will always have a power line to the west and the weather is cloudy but not overcast.

lm.name: RN16
lm.note:
Where : eastern Chaco, northwest of Resistencia, RN16

Description : Divided highway, the only one in Chaco, one of the lanes has danish road lines and the road may be a bit reddish.

lm.name: RN226
lm.note:
Where : southeastern Buenos Aires, between Balcarce and Mar del Plata, RN226

Description : Divided road that has tabletop hills with rocky ridge lines just like you will see in Lesotho.

lm.name: RN237
lm.note:
Where : southern Neuquén, south of Villa El Chocón, RN237

Description : Straight road with a lake visible south (most of the time). Has a shorter recognisable ridge north that can be useful if the lake isn't visible.

lm.name: RN251
lm.note:
Where : eastern Río Negro, north of General Conesa, RN251

Description : straight north to south road, danish road lines, sunset coverage, gets worse the further north you go.

lm.name: RN3
lm.note:
Where : eastern Río Negro, east of San Antonio Oeste, RN3

Description : Straight east to west angle, paved road. Powerline north which can help. Bushes might be bigger than expected since it is near the coast. Occasional sand dunes but not as often as the road to Bahia Creek.

lm.name: RN3
lm.note:
Where : southeastern Santa Cruz, west of Rio Gallegos, RN3

Description : East to west divided highway (southernmost in the world) with a small ridge north, overcast, lamps are common throughout this road too.

lm.name: RN3
lm.note:
Where : northeastern Chubut, between Puerto Madryn and Trelew, RN3

Description : Divided road with danish road lines on one lane. Coast is occasionally visible and therefore a good clue.

lm.name: RN3 (paved)
lm.note:
Where : Tierra del Fuego, between San Sebastián and Ushuaia, RN3

Description : Only major paved road in Tierra del Fuego, big mountains on the southern portion, slightly hilly and trees around Tolhuin, mostly overcast.

lm.name: RN3 (unpaved)
lm.note:
Where : southwestern Tierra del Fuego, west of Ushuaia, RN3

Description : Unpaved road, with a few cars passing by usually and a slightly larger road with the Ushuaia mountains visible commonly.

lm.name: RN34
lm.note:
Where : northern Salta, north of Tartagal, RN34

Description : Very dry looking with a distinct small ridge west and trafficked. Occasionally pink flower trees can be seen and palms.

lm.name: RN38
lm.note:
Where : central La Rioja, around La Rioja to Catamarca, RN38

Description : Big ridge to the west all the way through, flat to the east except in the northern part near Catamarca.

lm.name: RN40
lm.note:
Where : central La Rioja, west of Nonogasta, RN40

Description : Road running between very red mountains with green bushes covering them. The mountains are not as big as those south of Salta.

lm.name: RN40
lm.note:
Where : western Río Negro, south of San Carlos de Bariloche, RN40

Description : North south valley, with lots of yellow flowers in bushes, sometimes along a lake.

lm.name: RN40
lm.note:
Where : northern Jujuy, east of Ciénaga de Paicone, RN40

Description : Typical dry Jujuy landscape with reddish mountains and driving on the dried up river bed.

lm.name: RN40 (Gen3)
lm.note:
Where : southwestern Jujuy, south of Huáncar, RN40

Description : Only major Gen3 road left in Jujuy, road going through high altitude reddish hills.

lm.name: RN40 in Catamarca
lm.note:
Where : central Catamarca, RN40

Description : Car meta road (for the moment), only major mountainous road in western Argentina to have Striped car.

lm.name: RN52
lm.note:
Where : western Jujuy, around Susques, RN52

Description : Paved road going through high altitude hills and often has pinkish red soil and salt.

lm.name: RN52
lm.note:
Where : central Jujuy, around Santuario de Tres Pozos, RN52

Description : Road going through a salt pan. Very flat with mountains in the distance.

lm.name: RN60
lm.note:
Where : northern Catamarca, south of Las Peladas, RN60

Description : High altitude road that mostly goes through a narrower N-S valley and has salt, crushed volcanic rock and even a volcano visible in the north section.

lm.name: RN68
lm.note:
Where : southern Salta, north of Cafayate, RN68

Description : One of the most beautiful roads in Argentina. Has large exposed red rocky mountains and a dried up river bed visible in some areas.

lm.name: RN7
lm.note:
Where : western San Luis, west of San Luis, RN7

Description : East to west divided highway, with one lane concrete and one lane asphalt, the asphalt lane has danish road lines and lamps are commonly seen in the divide.

lm.name: RN7
lm.note:
Where : northwestern Mendoza, west of Upsallata, RN7

Description : Busy road, you’ll always see cars driving around, E-W valley, incredible mountains and snow coverage visible in the west.

lm.name: RN76
lm.note:
Where : northern La Rioja, north of Jagüé, RN76

Description : Unpaved road, high altitude red sandy hills (and sometimes more white ones). The red sandiness is different from the other high altitude roads mentioned in this guide.

lm.name: RN79
lm.note:
Where : southern Catamarca, around Olta, RN79

Description : SSE ridge, flat to the east, can be mistaken for the road around Villa San Agustin (R2 San Juan) however the ridge is slightly smaller here (here as in on the RN79).

lm.name: RN86
lm.note:
Where : northern Salta, east of Tartagal, RN86

Description : Very overcast road that is unpaved with brown soil, consistent angle and visible ridge if looking west down the road.

lm.name: Road to Villa de Merlo
lm.note:
Where : western Córdoba, east of Villa de Merlo

Description : Barren road due to the altitude, has dark rocks and occasional trees and a fence, winter coverage on a hilly plateau.

lm.name: Roads south of Resistencia
lm.note:
Where : southeastern Chaco, south of Resistencia

Description : Unpaved white sandy roads that are narrow with Caranday wax palms commonly but not always visible.

lm.name: RP1
lm.note:
Where : eastern Río Negro, on the coast east of Pozo Salado, RP1

Description : Road along the coast, water can rarely be seen south, otherwise you’ll be along a dune.

lm.name: RP1
lm.note:
Where : central Neuquén, north of Paso de los Indios, RP1

Description : Very red soil, unique overcast look, landscape going from very flat to hilly.

lm.name: RP11
lm.note:
Where : western Santa Cruz, west of El Calafate, RP11

Description : Concrete road wrapping around a mountain, with snow-capped mountains across a lake and snow near the road too.

lm.name: RP119
lm.note:
Where : southern Tierra del Fuego, south of Lago Fagnano, RP119

Description : Road on the side of a hill (hill is south) with occasional water with mountains across it visible north and southern Patagonian forest.

lm.name: RP153
lm.note:
Where : central Mendoza, north of Monte Comán, RP153

Description : Massive front blur, very flat, reddish road and has Mendoza specific pole tops commonly.

lm.name: RP173
lm.note:
Where : central Mendoza, southwest of San Rafael, RP173

Description : Massive front blur and road runs in an exposed dry rocky valley but has green vegetation and big trees and is trafficked.

lm.name: RP176
lm.note:
Where : northern Santiago del Estero, south of Nueva Esperanza, RP176

Description : Very straight north south road, paved, can be mistaken with the road south of Monte Quemado (R1 Santiago del Estero) however the grass here (here as in on the RP176) is of a way brighter green (and the car/copyright is different).

lm.name: RP21 & RP19
lm.note:
Where : western Santa Cruz, north of El Calafate, RP21/RP19

Description : Two unpaved roads along a lake either north or south (within Patagonia this configuration is mainly found on those two lakes, with only a few other smaller ones).

lm.name: RP23
lm.note:
Where : central Formosa, south of General Manuel Belgrano, RP23

Description : Very wide unpaved road with Caranday wax palms commonly.

lm.name: RP23
lm.note:
Where : western Neuquén, around Rahue, RP23

Description : North to south valley along a river, sometimes the river isn’t visible. Has a lot of trees for being this south in a valley and gen 4 in the north.

lm.name: RP23 & RP11
lm.note:
Where : western Santa Cruz, north of El Calafate, RP23/RP11

Description : Paved roads. The north road in the image can be recognised by the fact that it comes up really close to the mountains and has a lake south. The south road can be recognised because you can see snow-capped mountains across a glacial lake north.

lm.name: RP24 & RP3
lm.note:
Where : western Santiago del Estero, southwest of Santiago del Estero, RP24/RP3

Description : Very low ridge to the west and flatness to the east, the ridge is so small that it might not be visible sometimes.

lm.name: RP3
lm.note:
Where : central San Luis, from Nogolí to San Luis, RP3

Description : Divided by a ditch with curbs and has a rocky ridge to the east.

lm.name: RP30
lm.note:
Where : northern Santa Fe, just south of the border with Chaco, RP30

Description : Very narrow unpaved dirt road, going east to west, grey soil, very flat, sometimes palms can be seen.

lm.name: RP30
lm.note:
Where : eastern Chubut, west of Camarones, RP30

Description : Very snowy road on the west, sunset coverage on the east. The snow covers parts of the road which is different from the road to Fitz Roy.

lm.name: RP307
lm.note:
Where : western Tucuman, around El Mollar, RP307

Description : Tropical looking road, curb with white paint is the best clue to identify this road, trafficked and gets barren in the northern part due to the high altitude however the white painted curbs will still be present.

lm.name: RP33
lm.note:
Where : southern Catamarca, south of Catamarca, RP33

Description : Straight N-S road with an east ridge and has concrete poles on either side of the road. West also has a ridge closer to Catamarca. Gen 3 is very overcast.

lm.name: RP4
lm.note:
Where : central Catamarca, north of Catamarca, RP4

Description : North section is unpaved with pinkish soil and large bulbous green hills visible west. Further south the road is going through a green N-S valley.

lm.name: RP412
lm.note:
Where : western San Juan, north of Calingasta, RP412

Description : Very open valley in gen 3, sunny, small dry bushes, exposed ridges in every direction and is unpaved.

lm.name: RP43
lm.note:
Where : northeastern Santa Cruz, between Pico Truncado and Fitz Roy, RP43

Description : Melting snow on the side of the road, very straight and specific angle, paved. Does not have snow on the actual road but rather around it.

lm.name: RP43
lm.note:
Where : northwestern Santa Cruz, west of Perito Moreno, RP43

Description : Paved road with a dark blue lake north, very green vegetation can be seen as well.

lm.name: RP46
lm.note:
Where : central Catamarca, around Villa de Pomán, RP46

Description : Very large and distinct rocky ridge (larger than other ridges) sometimes very distant mountains visible west and ridge north in the northern section.

lm.name: RP46
lm.note:
Where : central Catamarca, north of Villa de Pomán, RP46

Description : East-west road cupped by mountains all around except south.

lm.name: RP47
lm.note:
Where : central Salta, southeast of Salta, RP47

Description : Pink soil, a portion is along a lake, red to pink exposed rocks with green dry vegetation in the east.

lm.name: RP5
lm.note:
Where : northern Jujuy, on the border with Salta, RP5

Description : High altitude road climbing into the clouds. That’s it.

lm.name: RP51
lm.note:
Where : western Córdoba, north of Villa Dolores, RP51

Description : Unpaved road with a wall of green dry bushes on either side and a ridge to the east that is sometimes barely visible. So look for it!

lm.name: RP510
lm.note:
Where : eastern San Juan, around Villa San Agustín, RP510

Description : SSE ridge to the west, with flatness east (sometimes a ridge can be seen very far).

lm.name: RP52
lm.note:
Where : northern Mendoza, north of the capital, RP52

Description : Concrete road, flatness southeast, ridges north and west.

lm.name: RP55 & RN148
lm.note:
Where : eastern San Luis, from Arizona to Villa de Merlo, RP55/RN148

Description : Mostly north to south divided road, with one lane concrete and one lane asphalt, a ridge can be seen east in the northern part. Has drier vegetation than the divided road in Entre Rios.

lm.name: RP60
lm.note:
Where : southern Río Negro, north of Cona Niyeu, RP60

Description : Mongolia-looking road ! Barely constitutes a road. Almost looks as if the driver veered off somewhere.

lm.name: RP61 North of Taco Pozo
lm.note:
Where : western Chaco, northeast of Taco Pozo, RP61

Description : Brown soil with a wall of dry green vegetation on either side. Animal footprints are commonly visible. Beware the N-S section of the road otherwise has a consistent road angle.

lm.name: RP92
lm.note:
Where : northern Santiago del Estero, south of Monte Quemado, RP92

Description : Very straight north south road, paved, road slightly wet, can be mistaken with the road south of Nueva Esperanza (R2 Santiago del Estero) however the grass on the R2 is of a way brighter green than this one (and the car/copyright is different).

lm.name: RPJ/K
lm.note:
Where : southern Tierra del Fuego, around Puerto Almanza, RPJ/K

Description : Road in between mountains, water south on the southern portion with southern Patagonian forest.

lm.name: Salta
lm.note:
Description : Salta has a very imposing ridge to the west and dry irregular hills to the east.

You will sometimes see elevation to the north and therefore might confuse it with Catamarca, but Salta is generally more dry-looking.

lm.name: San Juan
lm.note:
Description : San Juan will have big mountains to the west and a very flat ridge to the east (sometimes a ridge north is also visible). Vineyards are pretty common.

It is easily possible to confuse it with Mendoza however Mendoza won’t have a ridge to the east.

Moreover, San Juan does a lot of yellow (or red) painted bottom pole paint, which is rarer in Mendoza.

lm.name: San Luis
lm.note: Description : San Luis is the only major city with a big ridge to the east or northeast and flatness to the south and west.

lm.name: Sierra de La Ventana
lm.note:
Where : southwestern Buenos Aires, west of Sierra de La Ventana, RP76

Description : Overcast with a distinct dry, rocky ridge and pines commonly. Possibly even a bit New Zealand-esque to me. The south section is Gen 3 and has pale soil and the ridge is not always visible.

lm.name: Tucumán
lm.note: Description : San Miguel de Tucumán has a distinct tropical vibe, white stickers on most poles and a ridge west can sometimes be seen.

lm.name: Ushuaïa
lm.note: Description : Ushuaïa is by far the most distinct town in Argentina, with massive snow-capped mountains to the north.

lm.name: Villa Pehuenia
lm.note:
Where : western Neuquén, south of Villa Pehuenia

Description : Looks a lot like Chile and has monkey puzzle tree spam commonly.

lm.name: Volcán Diamante
lm.note:
Where : central Mendoza, west of San Rafael, roads around El Diamante

Description : A very distinct conical volcano which can be seen from very far.

lm.name: Volcán Tromen
lm.note:
Where : northern Neuquén, north of Chos Malal, roads around Volcán Tromen

Description : Very distinct volcano and has snow in Gen 4, but the POI is hard to find.

lm.name: 1 right dot dust - 1 right dot dust
lm.note: one dot on the back of the car on the right on this section of the 3 in Santa Cruz

lm.name: 251 road lines - 251 road lines
lm.note: The 251 has these Danish style roadlines. quite possibly the only non divided road in Arge with these roadlines. Also the northern part of the road has glitchy sunset coverage

lm.name: 3 smudge+dirt - RP29 3 Smudges + Dirt
lm.note: The RP29 in Santa Cruz has 3 smudges on the camera and is a dirt road. The RN40 also has these smudges but it is paved.

lm.name: 3 smudge+paved - RN40 3 Smudges Paved
lm.note: The RN40 (Bajo Caracoles <-> Perito Moreno) in Santa Cruz has 3 smudges on the camera. This is also seen on the RP29, but that road is dirt

lm.name: B type no top - B Type No Top
lm.note:
This is what I call a B type pole, featuring a lower bar with 2 insulator racks facing downwards and a one-sided bar above it with more down-facing insulators.

This is a variant of the B type pole where the vertical bar ends at the top horizontal bar unlike the standard version where it extends past it. Notably, (almost) every B Type pole in Buenos Aires Province will be of this variant. So if the vertical bar extends past the top horizontal bar, you will not be in BA. This is extremely helpful for regionguessing the central part of the country. Keep in mind that it can be found anywhere however, but by far the biggest cluster is in BA.

lm.name: B type short cap - B Type Variant - Short Cap
lm.note:
This is what I call a B type pole, featuring a lower bar with 2 insulator racks facing downwards and a one-sided bar above it with more down-facing insulators.

In this variant, there is a short cap immediately after the top horizontal beam. I have only ever seen this variant in Cordoba and La Rioja (credit to BCosign for spotting it in La Rioja, I had only seen it in Cordoba).

lm.name: B type standard top length - B Type Variant - Standard Length Top
lm.note:
This is what I call a B type pole, featuring a lower bar with 2 insulator racks facing downwards and a one-sided bar above it with more down-facing insulators.

In this variant, the vertical beam extends above the top horizontal bar at roughly about the same length between the two horizontal bars. This variant is most often found in Entre Rios and Santiago Del Estero and sometimes in Tucuman, Catamarca, and San Luis.

lm.name: beech forests - Beech Forests
lm.note: Beech forests are commonly found in the state of Tierra del Fuego.

lm.name: Butia yatay palm - Butia Yatay Palm
lm.note: The Butia yatay palm has arching, pinnate leaves and often grows at an incline with varying heights. It is most common in Corrientes and Parque Nacional El Palmar, Entre Rios.

lm.name: C type no cap - C Type No Cap
lm.note:
This is what I call a C Type Pole, where there are 3 alternating horizontal beams with down-facing insulators on the end of each of them. They are found everywhere with the exceptions of La Pampa (although a little Cordoba spill) and Misiones. More importantly, there are several region-specific variants.

This is probably the most useful variant, where there is no cap (but it still extends above). They can rarely be found scattered randomly, but are by far the most common in Cordoba Province and 2nd most common in BA (but still a lot more common in Cordoba).

lm.name: C type wide cap - C Type Variant - Wide Cap
lm.note:
This is what I call a C Type Pole, where there are 3 alternating horizontal beams with down-facing insulators on the end of each of them. They are found everywhere with the exceptions of La Pampa (although a little Cordoba spill) and Misiones. More importantly, there are several region-specific variants.

This is where there is a wide cap going both directions. It is most common in San Luis but can also be found more rarely in Cordoba.

lm.name: calden - Caldén
lm.note:
Prosopis caldenia, known as the caldén, is a decently large deciduous tree with small leaves and sinuous branches. It is mainly found in La Pampa.

NOTE: This tree can sometimes be confused with other trees such as the White Carob.

lm.name: Caranday palm - Caranday Palm
lm.note: Trithrinax Campestris, or the caranday palm, not to be confused with the Caranday Wax Palm, is a rustic palm native to the Sierras de Córdoba with a broader distribution in San Luis and northern mountainous Argentina. It can be identified by its compact fan-like leaves with a trunk hidden by a coat of dead-leaves.

lm.name: Caranday wax palm - Caranday wax palm
lm.note: Coperinicia alba, also known as the Caranday Wax Palm, have short, fan-like leaves that tend to grow in low-density, single-species forests. Most common in Formosa, they can also be found in Chaco, Corrientes and northern Santa Fe.

lm.name: cardon - Cardón
lm.note: Trichocereus atacamensis, or the cardón, is a cactus native to the high elevation mountain ranges of Catamarca, Tucumán, Salta and Jujuy. It can be identified by its candelabra-like appearance and fuzzy golden brown spines.

lm.name: center shape dust - center shape dust
lm.note: weird center smudge on the dust on the back of the car in chubut

lm.name: Comdoro Rivadavia -  Comodoro Rivadavia
lm.note: Comodoro Rivadavia is built on the slopes of Chenque hill, making the city recognisable.

lm.name: cordoba km marker - Cordoba KM Marker
lm.note: You can find these unique markers on provincial roads in Cordoba.

lm.name: cordoba mts - Cordoba Western Mountains
lm.note:
These mountains are typically found west of Córdoba.

NOTE: They are not as high as the mountains in the west.

lm.name: Cordoba sticker - Cordoba Sticker
lm.note:
Cordoba province has a very consistent back-of-sign sticker that appears as a red circle. It’s most commonly on the back of stop signs but appears on all sorts of other signs too like yield signs and even directional signs.

It seems to be relatively new (Gen 4 coverage has it, but 2013 Gen 3 doesn’t

lm.name: corn - Corn
lm.note: Corn fields can be found in most of northern Argentina, however they are most common in Córdoba, Buenos Aires and Santiago del Estero.

lm.name: Double V dust - Double V dust
lm.note: Double V looking dust on the back of the car

lm.name: flat barren landscape - Flat Barren Landscape
lm.note: Flat and barren landscapes like this are typically found in central southern Argentina.

lm.name: flat barren red soil - flat barren red soil
lm.note: Red soil with a barren landscape and mountain ranges, can often be seen on the RN76 in Parque Nacional Talampaya in western La Rioja.

lm.name: flat grass+ no bushes - flat grass+ no bushes
lm.note: If you see this kind of vegetation with flat grass and a low number of bushes, you are almost certainly in the state of Tierra del Fuego or southeastern Santa Cruz.

lm.name: gen 4 volcanic rocs - gen 4 volcanic rocks
lm.note: These volcanic rocks in Generation 4 coverage can only be found on the RP43 south of Antofagasta de la Sierra in northwestern Catamarca.

lm.name: Grassland - Grassland
lm.note: Grassland with a few separated tree plantations is generally found in this area.

lm.name: IOMF poletop Corrientes - IOMF poletop Corrientes
lm.note: "Isle Of Man Flag" style poletop. Corrientes Variant (vertical bar barely goes above the top, if at all)

lm.name: IOMF poletop Jujuy - IOMF poletop Jujuy
lm.note: "Isle Of Man Flag" style poletop. Jujuy + Misiones Variant (vertical bar goes far above the top)

lm.name: IOMF poletop Misiones - IOMF poletop Misiones
lm.note: "Isle Of Man Flag" style poletop. Jujuy + Misiones Variant (vertical bar goes far above the top)

lm.name: IOMF poletop San Luis - IOMF poletop San Luis
lm.note: "Isle Of Man Flag" style poletop. San Luis Variant (vertical bar goes a bit above the top)

lm.name: la pampa t junction - La Pampa T-Junction
lm.note: T-Junctions in La Pampa sometimes have these yellow rectangular signs, with a chevron pattern on the bottom, and the Road Number(s) above, with an arrow on both sides.

lm.name: latvian poles - Latvian Poles
lm.note: Within Argentina, these Latvian style wooden hook poles are unique to La Rioja and Mendoza. (mendoza is kinda fake its basically only La Rioja)

lm.name: left 3 stripes dust - left 3 stripes dust
lm.note: 3 stripes on the left back of the car. Might be found on some other roads in this general area of East Chubut but from what I see most of it is now Gen 4.

lm.name: macaw palm - Macaw Palm
lm.note: The Macaw Palm has small thin leaves with a visible spear shaped top. It can be found as a decorational plant all across Argentina, however in the wild it is most common in Formosa, Chaco and Misiones.

lm.name: mar del plata architecture - Mar Del Plata Architecture
lm.note: In Mar Del Plata and surrounding cities (such as Miramar and Necochea), a unique style of architecture can be found. Its main features include quartzite stoned facades, orange tiled roofs, attached garages, and vault shaped porches.

lm.name: mendoza single insulator - mendoza single insulator
lm.note: In Mendoza, poles with a single insulator attached to the side of the pole can be found.

lm.name: mendoza vinyards - Mendoza Vineyards
lm.note:
If you see vineyards with mountains in the west and flatness in the east, you are most likely in the outskirts of Mendoza.

NOTE: There are multiple wine regions in Argentina, but the Mendoza wine region is the most recognisable one of them all.

lm.name: monkey puzzle - Monkey Puzzle Tree
lm.note:
The monkey puzzle tree can be found in western Neuquen. The most specimens are seen on state road 23.

NOTE: They are seen on the other side in Chile as well.

lm.name: Pampas grass - Pampas Grass
lm.note: Pampas grass (Cortaderia selloana) is one of the most defining flora of the Pampas region. It is recognizable by its long bunched reeds and white fluffy flowerheads.

lm.name: pink trumpet tree - Pink Trumpet Tree
lm.note: The Pink Trumpet Tree (Handroanthus impetiginosus) can be found in cities in northern Salta such as Orán, Tartagal and General Mosconi.

lm.name: red brick - Red Brick
lm.note: Red bricks, similar to what is common in Bolivia, can be found in the northwest of the country, especially in western Jujuy.

lm.name: red rock formations - Red Rock Formations+Dam
lm.note:
Villa Dique Florentino Ameghino in northeastern Chubut is surrounded by these rock formations.

NOTE: Sometimes you will be able to see this dam in the west.

lm.name: Red soil - Red Soil
lm.note:
Red soil is typically found in the Misiones province.

NOTE: Brazil and Argentina can look similar in this region. Make sure to look for other clues first.

lm.name: redish road+needlegrass - reddish road+needle-grass
lm.note: Roads with reddish pavement lined with long Argentine needle-grass are common in San Luis.

lm.name: rio colorado sunrise - rio colorado sunrise
lm.note: Sunrise coverage with bad image quality and multiple blurs is found on a short part of the RN251 and RN22, west of Río Colorado. (the 22 might be overwritten w/ new coverage)

lm.name: RN16 - RN16 Danish Roadlines
lm.note: The RN16 has danish style Roadlines. There are a handful of roads that have this in Arge. What makes this one unique is it is divided, and the inner line is yellow. The RN16 also meets this criteria, so use the road angle to determine which is which.

lm.name: rn40 sunrise - RN40 Sunrise
lm.note:
Sunrise coverage with degraded image quality is found on the RN40 just south of the Mendoza border with Neuquén.

NOTE: The quality of the coverage improves closer to the border.

lm.name: rn65 - RN65 "death road"
lm.note:
The western part of the RN65 in western Tucumán can easily be recognized by this small, dangerous road in the clouds.

NOTE: This road can look similar to the “Road of Death” in Bolivia.

lm.name: rn68 red hills - RN68 Red Hills
lm.note: These red mountains are unique to the RN68 valley in southern Salta.

lm.name: RN7 - RN7 Danish Roadliens
lm.note: The RN 7 has Danish syle roadlines. There are a handful of roads with Danish Roadlines. What makes this one unique is it is divided, and the inner line is yellow. The only other road that meets this criteria is the R16, but they look different and you can use the road angle to determine which is which.

lm.name: RN9 Rosario  - RN9 Rosario-BA Danish Roadlines
lm.note: The RN9 from Rosario to (roughly) Buenos Aires has danish style outer lines. What makes this one unique is it is divided, and both the outer and inner line are white.

lm.name: rp25 snow coverage - RP25 Snow Coverage
lm.note: This snow coverage is found on the eastern RP25 in eastern Santa Cruz.

lm.name: rp293 - RN293
lm.note: Melting snow coverage is seen on the eastern RN293 close to the Chilean border in southwestern Santa Cruz.

lm.name: salt pans - Salt Pans
lm.note:
Salt pans in Argentina are typically found in Jujuy.

NOTE: They can also be found in southwestern Bolivia and northeastern Chile, but without Generation 4 coverage.

lm.name: Sandy soil + vegetation - Sandy soil + vegetation
lm.note: In the Chaco and Formosa provinces, you will often see sandy soil with an abundance of vegetation; mainly low trees and bushes.

lm.name: sawdust car - Sawdust Car
lm.note: The “sawdust” car is found in centre-south Argentina and has a unique sandy dust on its visible black back.

lm.name: semi coastal grassy hills - semi coastal grassy hills
lm.note: Semi-coastal grass hills are seen in southern Buenos Aires, especially northeast of Bahía Blanca.

lm.name: small lakes - Small Lakes
lm.note: Small lakes near the road are occasionally seen in the province of Buenos Aires.

lm.name: sorghum - Sorghum
lm.note: Fields of sorghum can most commonly be seen in Santa Fe, Córdoba and Buenos Aires. It can be identified by its dark red flowerheads.

lm.name: sugarcane - Sugarcane plantations
lm.note: Sugarcane plantations are most common in Tucumán, with hotspots appearing in Salta and Jujuy.

lm.name: sunflower fields - Sunflower Fields
lm.note: Fields of sunflowers are mainly found in southern Chaco, and less commonly in Buenos Aires and southern Córdoba.

lm.name: Thick Slanted Stripes dust - Thick Slanted Stripes dust
lm.note: Thick Slanted Stripes smudged into the back of the car in Santa Cruz

lm.name: toothpick cactus - Toothpick Cactus
lm.note: Stetsonia coryne, or the toothpick cactus, is a large tree-like cactus with many branches and spines resembling toothpicks. Its habitat includes a hotspot between Catamarca and Cordoba as well as the border area between Chaco, Salta and Formosa.

lm.name: tree plantations - Tree Plantations
lm.note:
The majority of tree plantations in Argentina are located in the Entre Rios province.

NOTE: Uruguay and southern Brazil have them as well. Make sure to look at other clues before guessing.

lm.name: Tucuman pole sticker - Tucuman pole stickers
lm.note: White vertical pole stickers with several digits can be found in Tucumán.

lm.name: upside down trident pole - upside down trident pole
lm.note: This upside-down trident pole with a diagonal extension is unique to Misiones Province.

lm.name: ushuaia - Ushuaia
lm.note:
These snowy mountains to the north can only be found in Ushuaia.

NOTE: Ushuaia is the southernmost city of Argentina and the province capital of Tierra del Fuego.

lm.name: Valdes Peninsula - Valdes Peninsula
lm.note: Unusually wide dirt roads and flat geography make the Valdes peninsula of Eastern Chubut recognizable.

lm.name: Western mountains - Far West Mountains
lm.note:
Far western Argentina typically features a mountainous landscape.

NOTE: It is rare to find mountains in eastern Argentina.

lm.name: wild sunflowers - Wild Sunflower
lm.note: Wild sunflowers (Verbesina encelioides) are often found in Salta, Jujuy and Tucumán.

lm.name: B Type - cap
lm.note: B Type with a cap on top featuring a lower bar with 2 insulator racks facing downwards and a one-sided bar above it with more down-facing insulators.

lm.name: B Type - insulators facing Up
lm.note: B-Type with insulators facing up featuring a lower bar with 2 insulator racks facing upwards and a one-sided bar above it with more up-facing insulators.

lm.name: B Type - no top
lm.note: This is a variant of the B type pole where the vertical bar ends at the top horizontal bar unlike the standard version where it extends past it.

lm.name: B Type - short top
lm.note: B-Type short top - In this variant, the vertical bar only extends a very small amount past the top horizontal bar, less than the length between the two horizontal bars.

lm.name: B Type - standard length top
lm.note: In this variant, the vertical beam extends above the top horizontal bar at roughly about the same length between the two horizontal bars.

lm.name: B Type - wooden
lm.note: A wooden variant of the B Type pole.

lm.name: C Type - no cap
lm.note: C Type Pole, where there are 3 alternating horizontal beams with down-facing insulators on the end of each of them. In this variant there is no cap on top.

lm.name: C Type - short cap
lm.note: Short cap is where the vertical beam extends above the top horizontal bar a distance less than the distance less than the distance between the other horizontal beams.

lm.name: D Type
lm.note: It has no other horizontal beams except the one on top which has a unique shape to the other types of poles in Argentina. It can be found everywhere but there are region where there less common.

lm.name: silver plate
lm.note: White vertical pole stickers with several digits can be found in Tucumán.

lm.name: single insulator
lm.note: In Mendoza, poles with a single insulator attached to the side of the pole can be found.

lm.name: wooden hook poles
lm.note: Within Argentina, these Latvian style wooden hook poles are unique to La Rioja and Mendoza.

top.html:
Argentina uses two types of licence plates: a black one, which will be visible on street view with a black dot in the middle, and a white one with a blue bar at the top.

NOTE: The black dot can only be found on Argentinian licence plates, while the blue bar can be found in Brazil as well.

NOTE: The black dot can only be found on Argentinian licence plates, while the blue bar can be found in Brazil as well.

top.html:
Argentina has a black Google car in Generation 3 coverage.

NOTE: Within South America, only Argentina, Peru and Uruguay have a black Google car.

NOTE: Peru, Brazil and Argentina are the only South American countries with smallcam.

top.html:
Round concrete poles sustaining three electricity lines in an alternating pattern are very common in Argentina.

Doubled up poles like in the second image is also a good clue for Argentina.

NOTE: Similar doubled concrete poles can occasionally be found throughout Bolivia.

NOTE: Similar doubled concrete poles can occasionally be found throughout [Bolivia](https://goo.gl/maps/9soPnAuBufSD1GmH7).

top.html:
Wooden poles are somewhat common in Argentina, they can be found either with a crossbar or without.

NOTE: Wooden A-frame poles in South America are only found in Argentina.

top.html:
Argentina typically uses white-and-red chevrons.

NOTE: Argentina is the only American country with these chevrons.
top.raw: Argentina typically uses **white-and-red** chevrons. NOTE: Argentina is the only American country with these chevrons.

top.html: Road lines in Argentina are mainly dashed white, double yellow or a mix in between.
top.raw: Road lines in Argentina are mainly dashed** white**, double** yellow** or a mix in between.

top.html:
Argentinian kilometre markers are typically white with a black strip displaying the road number at the top.

NOTE: The markers on national highways are indicated with RN, while RP indicates a provincial highway. National highways will be labelled white on the map, while provincial highways will be labelled green.

NOTE: The markers on national highways are indicated with RN, while RP indicates a provincial highway. National highways will be labelled white on the map, while provincial highways will be labelled green.

top.html:
Yellow and red rectangular reflectors can often be seen on Argentinian guardrails.

NOTE: Within South America, they can also be found in Uruguay. However, Uruguayan guardrails can be differentiated from Argentinian guardrails by the shape of their support.
top.raw: **Yellow and red rectangular reflectors** can often be seen on Argentinian guardrails. NOTE: Within South America, they can also be found in Uruguay.** **However, Uruguayan guardrails can be differentiated from Argentinian guardrails by the shape of their [support](/images/argentina/argentinauruguay_guardrailsupport.jpg).

top.html: While Argentina features a plethora of different landscapes, most of the country is relatively flat, mostly treeless, and sparsely populated. In the absence of better clues, you should consider Argentina when you see landscapes like this with a very “wide open”, desolate feel.
